'''Baden Powell''', [[Master of Arts (Oxbridge)|MA]] [[Royal Society|FRS]] [[Royal Geographical Society|FRGS]] (22 August 1796 – 11 June 1860)<ref>GRO Register of Deaths: Jun 1860 1a 38 Kensington – Baden Powell, age unknown</ref> was an English [[mathematician]] and [[Church of England]] priest. He held the [[Savilian Professor of Geometry|Savilian Chair of Geometry]] at the [[University of Oxford]] from 1827 to 1860. Powell was a prominent [[Liberal Christianity|liberal theologian]] who put forward advanced ideas about [[evolution]].

==Origins==
Baden Powell II was born at [[Stamford Hill]], [[Hackney, London|Hackney]] in [[London]].<ref name="Oxford University Press">{{cite book |last1=Corsi |first1=Pietro |title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |publisher=Oxford University Press |ref=Powell, Baden}}</ref> His father, Baden Powell I (1767–1841), of Langton and Speldhurst in Kent, was a wine merchant,<ref name="Oxford University Press"/> who served as [[High Sheriff]] of [[Kent]] in 1831, and as Master of the [[Worshipful Company of Mercers]] in 1822.<ref>Edgar Powell, Pedigree of the Families of Powell and Baden-Powwll, London, 1926, pedigree chart p.xi [https://www.seekingmyroots.com/members/files/G005202.pdf]</ref> The mother of Baden Powell II was Hester Powell (1776–1848), his father's paternal first cousin,<ref name="Oxford University Press"/><ref name="ReferenceB"/> a daughter of James Powell (1737–1824) of Clapton, Hackney, Middlesex, Master of the [[Worshipful Company of Salters]] in 1818.<ref name="Edgar Powell, pedigree chart, p.xi">Edgar Powell, pedigree chart, p.xi</ref>

The Powell family can be traced back to the early 16th century, where they were yeomen farmers at [[Mildenhall, Suffolk|Mildenhall]] in Suffolk.<ref name="Edgar Powell, pedigree chart, p.xi"/> Baden Powell's eleventh great-grandfather, David Powell (1725–1810) of Homerton, Middlesex,<ref name="Edgar Powell, pedigree chart, p.xi"/> a second son, migrated to the [[City of London]] aged 17 in 1712, subsequently going into business as a merchant at [[Broad Street (ward)|Old Broad Street]] and buying the manor of [[Wattisfield]] in Suffolk.<ref>Burke's Peerage, Baronetage and Knightage, 106th edition, vol. 1, ed. Charles Mosley, Burke's Peerage Ltd, p. 159</ref><ref name="ReferenceB">{{Cite web|title=The Powell Pedigree {{!}} Home|url=https://www.spanglefish.com/ThePowellPedigree/|access-date=2020-07-01|website=spanglefish.com}}</ref> In 1740 a branch of the family bought the [[Whitefriars Glass]] works.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Whitefriars Glass History – Boha Glass|url=https://www.bohaglass.co.uk/whitefriars-glass-history/|access-date=2020-07-01|website=bohaglass.co.uk|date=2 January 2017 }}</ref>

The name Baden originated in Susanna Baden (1663–1737), the maternal grandmother of David Powell (1725–1810) of Homerton, Middlesex,<ref name="Edgar Powell, pedigree chart, p.xi"/> and one of the ten children of Andrew Baden (1637–1716), a Mercer who served as Mayor of Salisbury in 1682.<ref>Edgar Powell, p.39</ref>

==Education==
Powell was admitted as an undergraduate at [[Oriel College, Oxford]] in 1814,<ref>{{alox2|title=Powell, Baden}}</ref> and graduated with a first-class honours degree in mathematics in 1817.<ref name="Oxford University Press"/>

==Ordination==
Powell was ordained as a priest of the Church of England in 1821, having served as curate of [[Midhurst]], [[Sussex]].<ref name="Oxford University Press"/> His first living was as Vicar of [[Plumstead]], Kent, of which the [[advowson]] was owned by his family.<ref name="Oxford University Press"/> He immediately began his scientific work there, starting with experiments on radiant heat.<ref name="Oxford University Press"/>

==Marriages and children==
[[File:Grave of Baden Powell and family, Kensal Green Cemetery, February 2024.jpg|thumb|right|Powell's grave at [[Kensal Green Cemetery]]]]
Powell married three times, and had fourteen children in total. His widow changed the last name of the surviving children of his third marriage to "Baden-Powell".<ref>Edrar Powell, p.14</ref>

Powell's first marriage on 21 July 1821 to Eliza Rivaz (died 13 March 1836) was childless.

His second marriage on 27 September 1837 to Charlotte Pope (died 14 October 1844) produced one son and three daughters:
* Charlotte Elizabeth Powell, (14 September 1838&ndash;20 October 1917)
* [[Baden Henry Powell|Baden Henry Baden-Powell]], [[FRSE]] (23 August 1841&ndash;2 January 1901)
* Louisa Ann Powell, (18 March 1843&ndash;1 August 1896)
* Laetitia Mary Powell, (4 June 1844&ndash;2 September 1865)

[[File:Baden Powell family.jpg|Survivors of Baden Powell's third family: Back row, standing (left to right): Major B. F. S. Baden-Powell; Miss Agnes D. S. Baden-Powell; Mr. Frank Baden-Powell; Colonel R. S. S. Baden-Powell. Front row, seated: Sir George Baden-Powell; Mrs. Henrietta Grace Baden-Powell with one of Powell's grandchildren; and Mr. Warington Baden-Powell|thumb]]
His third marriage on 10 March 1846 (at [[St Luke's Church, Chelsea]]) to Henrietta Grace Smyth (3 September 1824&ndash;13 October 1914), a daughter of [[William Henry Smyth|Admiral Smyth]], produced seven sons and three daughters:
* [[Warington Baden-Powell|Henry Warington Baden-Powell]], (3 February 1847&ndash;24 April 1921), a naval officer, a fellow of the [[Royal Geographical Society]] and a King's Counsel (K.C.)
* Sir [[George Baden-Powell|George Smyth Baden-Powell]], (24 December 1847&ndash;20 November 1898), a politician and Conservative MP (1885–1898)
* Augustus Smyth Powell (1849&ndash;1863)
* [[Frank Baden-Powell|Francis (Frank) Smyth Baden-Powell]] (29 July 1850&ndash; 25 December 1933),<ref>B-P's diary transcribed by Colin Walker</ref> an artist who exhibited at the [[Royal Academy of Arts]]
* Henrietta Smyth Powell (28 October 1851&ndash;9 March 1854)
* John Penrose Smyth Powell (21 December 1852&ndash;14 December 1855)
* Jessie Smyth Powell (25 November 1855&ndash;24 July 1856)
* [[Robert Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell|Robert Stephenson Smyth Baden-Powell, 1st Baron Baden-Powell]], (22 February 1857&ndash;8 January 1941), an army officer, writer and a founder of the [[scouting|World Scouting Movement]] and (with his sister Agnes) founder of the [[Girlguiding UK|Girl Guides]].
* [[Agnes Baden-Powell|Agnes Smyth Baden-Powell]], (16 December 1858&ndash;2 June 1945), founder of the [[Girlguiding UK|Girl Guides]].
* [[Baden Baden-Powell|Baden Fletcher Smyth Baden-Powell]], (22 May 1860&ndash;3 October 1937), an army officer, aviator and president of the [[Royal Aeronautical Society]]

Shortly after Powell's death in 1860, his wife renamed the remaining children of his third marriage 'Baden-Powell'; the name was eventually legally changed by royal licence on 30 April 1902.<ref>Charles Mosley, editor, Burke's Peerage and Baronetage, 106th edition, 2 volumes (Crans, Switzerland: Burke's Peerage (Genealogical Books) Ltd, 1999), volume 1, page 159.</ref> Baden Henry Powell is often also referred to as Baden Henry Baden-Powell,<ref>[http://catalog.loc.gov/cgi-bin/Pwebrecon.cgi?DB=local&Search_Arg=Baden+Henry+Powell&Search_Code=NAME%40&CNT=100 Books of Baden Henry Powell in The Library of Congress]</ref> and was using this name by the 1891 census.

== Evolution ==
Powell was an outspoken advocate of the constant uniformity of the laws of the material world. His views were liberal, and he was sympathetic to [[evolutionary]] theory long before [[Charles Darwin]] had revealed his ideas. He argued that science should not be placed next to scripture or the two approaches would conflict, and in his own version of [[Francis Bacon]]'s dictum, contended that the book of God's works was separate from the book of God's word, claiming that moral and physical phenomena were completely independent.<ref name=young>{{cite web |url=http://www.human-nature.com/dm/chap1.html |title=The impact of Darwin on conventional thought|access-date=2007-08-29 |author=Robert M. Young |author-link=Robert M. Young (academic) |year=1985 |work=Darwin's Metaphor: Nature's Place in Victorian Culture | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070930154654/http://www.human-nature.com/dm/chap1.html| archive-date= 30 September 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref>

His faith in the [[Uniformitarianism|uniformity of nature]] (except man's mind) was set out in a [[theology|theological]] argument; if God is a lawgiver, then a "miracle" would break the lawful edicts that had been issued at Creation. Therefore, a belief in miracles would be entirely atheistic.<ref name="ReferenceA">{{harvnb|Desmond|Moore|1991|p=500}}</ref> Powell's most significant works defended, in succession, the [[uniformitarianism (science)|uniformitarian geology]] set out by [[Charles Lyell]] and the evolutionary ideas in ''[[Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation]]'' published anonymously by [[Robert Chambers (journalist)|Robert Chambers]] which applied uniform laws to the history of life in contrast to more respectable ideas such as [[catastrophism]] involving a series of divine creations.<ref name=young/> "He insisted that no tortured interpretation of [[Book of Genesis|Genesis]] would ever suffice; we had to let go of the [[Genesis creation myth|Days of Creation]] and base [[Christianity]] on the moral laws of the [[New Testament]]."<ref>Desmond, Adrian 1982. ''Archetypes and ancestors''. Muller, London. p45</ref>

The boldness of Powell and other theologians in dealing with science led [[Joseph Dalton Hooker]] to comment in a letter to [[Asa Gray]] dated 29 March 1857: "These parsons are so in the habit of dealing with the abstractions of doctrines as if there was no difficulty about them whatever, so confident, from the practice of having the talk all to themselves for an hour at least every week with no one to gainsay a syllable they utter, be it ever so loose or bad, that they gallop over the course when their field is Botany or Geology as if we were in the pews and they in the pulpit. Witness the self-confident style of Whewell and Baden Powell, Sedgwick and Buckland." [[William Whewell]], [[Adam Sedgwick]] and [[William Buckland]] opposed evolutionary ideas.<ref>{{harvnb|Desmond|Moore|1991|p=412}}<br />Huxley, Leonard 1918. ''[https://archive.org/stream/lifelettersofsir01hookrich/lifelettersofsir01hookrich_djvu.txt Life and letters of Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker OM GCSI]''. London, Murray. pp. 477–478</ref>

When the idea of [[natural selection]] was opened to debate by Charles Darwin and [[Alfred Russel Wallace]] in their 1858 papers to the [[Linnaean Society]], both Powell and his brother-in-law<ref>Flower married Georgiana Rosetta Smyth, younger sister of Henrietta Grace Smyth, on 15 April 1858.</ref> [[William Henry Flower]] thought that natural selection made creation rational.<ref>Desmond, Adrian 1982. ''Archetypes and ancestors''. Muller, London. p51 et seq 'The Christian commitment'.</ref>

{{blockquote|The 'Philosophy of Creation' has been treated in a masterly manner by the Rev. Baden Powell, in his 'Essays on the Unity of Worlds,' 1855. Nothing can be more striking than the manner in which he shows that the introduction of new species is "a regular, not a casual phenomenon," or, as Sir John Herschel expresses it, "a natural in contra-distinction to a miraculous process."<ref>{{harvnb|Darwin|1861|p=[http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?viewtype=text&itemID=F381&pageseq=25 xviii]}}</ref>}}

==''Essays and Reviews''==
He was one of seven liberal theologians who produced a manifesto titled ''[[Essays and Reviews]]'' around February 1860, which amongst other things joined in the debate over ''[[On the Origin of Species]]''. These [[Anglican]]s included Oxford professors, country clergymen, the headmaster of [[Rugby school]] and a layman. Their declaration that miracles were irrational stirred up unprecedented anger, drawing much of the fire away from Charles Darwin. ''Essays'' sold 22,000 copies in two years, more than the ''Origin'' sold in twenty years, and sparked five years of increasingly polarised debate with books and pamphlets furiously contesting the issues.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>

Referring to "Mr Darwin's masterly volume" and restating his argument that belief in miracles is atheistic, Baden Powell wrote that the book "must soon bring about an entire revolution in opinion in favour of the grand principle of the self-evolving powers of nature.":
{{blockquote|Just a similar scepticism has been evinced by nearly all the first physiologists of the day, who have joined in rejecting the development theories of Lamarck and the Vestiges; and while they have strenuously maintained successive creations, have denied strenuously maintained successive creations, have denied and denounced the alleged production of organic life by Messrs. Crosse and Weekes, and stoutly maintained the impossibility of spontaneious generation, on the alleged ground of contradiction to experience. Yet it is now acknowledged under the high sanction of the name of Owen (British Association Address 1858), that 'creation' is only another name for our ignorance of the mode of production; and it has been the unanswered and unanswerable argument of another reasoner that new species must have originated either out of their inorganic elements, or out of previously organized forms; either development or spontaneous generation must be true: while a work has now appeared by a naturalist of the most acknowledged authority, Mr. Darwin's masterly volume on The Origin of Species by the law of 'natural selection' – which now substantiates on undeniable grounds the very principle so long denounced by the first naturalist – the origination of new species by natural causes: a work which must soon bring about an entire revolution of opinion in favour of the grand principle of the self-evolving powers of nature.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://lachlan.bluehaze.com.au/1860-essays-reviews/index.html |title=The 1860 publication: "Essays and Reviews" by (Church of England theologians) Temple, Williams, Powell, Wilson, Goodwin, Pattison and Jowett |access-date=2007-08-29 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20070830032106/http://lachlan.bluehaze.com.au/1860-essays-reviews/index.html| archive-date= 30 August 2007 | url-status= live}}</ref> }}

He would have been on the platform at the [[British Association for the Advancement of Science]] [[1860 Oxford evolution debate]] that was a highlight of the [[reaction to Darwin's theory]]. [[Thomas Henry Huxley|Huxley]]'s antagonist [[Samuel Wilberforce|Wilberforce]] was also the foremost critic of ''Essays and Reviews''. Powell died of a heart attack a fortnight before the meeting.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> He is buried in [[Kensal Green Cemetery]], London.

== Notable students ==
